title: In those days (Luke 2:1–7)
hookLine: an emperor counts his people, and God arrives uncounted

lines: A DECREE GOES OUT FROM ROME.
JOSEPH, AND MARY GREAT WITH CHILD.
cards: Somewhere in Rome, an order goes out: count everyone, so the empire knows who it can tax. It's the kind of thing powerful people do without thinking twice: a line in a decree, and ordinary lives rearranged.
Families pack up and go, each to their own city, to be registered.

Among them, walking from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, are Joseph, of the house of David, and Mary, the young woman he's engaged to, great with child. The emperor will never hear their names.
He's counting heads, not looking at faces.

teach.b: Luke opens the scene like a history book, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed."
Some readers puzzle over how this census fits other records of the time, and Luke doesn't stop to explain. He cares about the contrast.
The emperor's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town, little Bethlehem from Micah, without the emperor ever knowing.

Then the birth, in two verses: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No angels yet, no star.
A feeding trough for a crib. And notice what isn't there: no innkeeper. Nobody slams a door.
Luke's Greek word for inn is the one he uses later for the guestchamber where Jesus eats the Passover with his friends.

teach.h: NO INNKEEPER: A FULL GUEST ROOM.
teach.b: So some scholars picture a family house with its guest room already full, and the baby laid where the animals fed.

teach.h: THE CENTER COUNTS; GOD COMES TO THE EDGE.
teach.b: The emperor sits at the center of the world, counting.

teach.h: THERE WAS NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.
teach.b: In the Christian telling, God arrives at its edge, uncounted, in a crowded place, in a feeding trough. Some see a hint of the end of Luke's story, when his body is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb hewn in stone.

how: Luke 2:1–20 is a Christmas reading in churches, and some families read it aloud at home on Christmas Eve or at the Christmas table.

games.q: what's inside Luke 2:1–7 — tap the pairs.

s: Luke's story has an innkeeper who turns them away
no innkeeper appears. the text says only there was no room for them in the inn, perhaps a guest room.
Luke describes the birth itself in very few words
two verses: she brought forth her son, wrapped him and laid him in a manger.
Luke's word for inn is used again for the room of the Last Supper
the same Greek word, kataluma, names the guest chamber in Luke 22.

games.q: you're Joseph, in Bethlehem with Mary about to give birth, and the guest room is full. where is the baby laid?
o: in a manger, a feeding trough.
games.why: she "laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." a feeding trough for a crib.

practice: Think of the biggest story in today's news, big names, big numbers, and look underneath it for the people at its edges who'll never be named: a family packing up, a nurse on a night shift, a child somewhere in the crowd.
Pick one and hold them in mind for a moment, by face, not by number. If you pray, pray for them; if not, simply let them matter to you for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Kataluma, Luke's Greek word for a guest room, usually translated inn: the opening of his birth story, where an emperor counts the world and Jesus is born at its edge, laid in a manger.

orig.note: Greek: a lodging, a guest room. usually translated inn in Luke 2:7, and guestchamber in Luke 22:11.

carryVoice: Your line: not counted, but there. Born at the edge, where the animals fed. See you tomorrow.
